messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Chidi was thirty-three, a social media manager in Chicago, married for five years to a woman who still looked at him with concern he couldn’t meet. Two years earlier he had been a relief worker in a war zone, distributing supplies in a town that changed hands three times in six weeks. The day that undid him began like the others—a line of families, dust and diesel, the high whine of generators—until a mortar round hit the distribution point fifty yards away. He was knocked flat by the shockwave; when he sat up, there was a boy’s shoe on the ground beside him, still laced, and a woman nearby whose face he could not remember afterward except as a sound. He helped carry wounded, but the people who fired the mortar were never identified, let alone held accountable. That absence of consequence lodged in him like a splinter: no one had answered for it, and the more he turned it over, the more he felt the world was a place where terrible things happened and nothing was set right.  

Back home, the injustice stayed with him. He believed the attack had been deeply unfair, and the fact that no one faced consequences made him certain that danger could come at any moment, from any direction, without warning. He started scanning every environment before he entered it—checking corners, watching hands, noticing exits. His hypervigilance became automatic; he would catch himself flinching at a car backfiring, or freezing when a delivery truck growled too close to the curb. At work, managing a brand’s social feed meant scrolling through thousands of pieces of content daily. A single thumbnail of a dusty street or a blurry explosion would lock his concentration until he was aware only of his heart and the small black edge of panic. He found it almost impossible to concentrate on simple captions or analytics because his attention kept drifting to ambient sounds—a dropped keyboard, a colleague’s laughter—any of which could be the first note of something worse.  

He tried to manage the vigilance by pushing the memories away. When a thought of the boy’s shoe surfaced, he forced it down; when he felt the startle rising at a sudden noise, he told himself not to think about it. He detached from the memories as if they belonged to someone else, a stranger he was responsible for but did not want to know. For a few months this seemed to work. But the strategy backfired: the more he avoided thinking about the event, the more his threat system stayed on high alert, as if the unprocessed material leaked into his surroundings. His scanning intensified—he checked the rearview mirror repeatedly while driving, and at night he would get up to walk the apartment, listening. His wife would wake and ask what he was doing, and he would say he was checking the locks, but really he was checking for the shape of something he could not name.  

The cycle tightened. Because he could not rely on himself to stay calm—he felt he might lose control, might scream or run in a meeting—he relied even more on scanning, on avoidance, on the hollow ritual of detachment. Each time he suppressed a memory, his hypervigilance spiked; each spike made him more certain that he could not trust his own mind, which fed the sense that the world was still unfair and unaccountable, and that he was alone in his response to it. His startle response became so pronounced that a colleague touching his shoulder sent him nearly out of his chair. He started wearing headphones at his desk, partly to concentrate but mostly to control what he heard.  

He came to therapy because his wife, gently, told him she could not live with someone who was always braced for an explosion that might never come. He was afraid, though, that she was wrong—that the explosion would come, and he would be the only one who saw it, frozen by the memory of a boy’s shoe and a face he could not fully remember.
